briefdescription.para: The quadrature rule the consistent mass of an element of the given shape is integrated with: the full Gauss rule of that shape.
The element quadrature point nearest to a point of the mass rule, in parent coordinates.

parameterdescription.para: A container of the element's quadrature points, each with a member xi holding its parent coordinates.
Parent coordinates of the point of the mass rule.

simplesect.para: The index of the nearest one; the first of them on a tie.

briefdescription.para: The quadrature of the consistent mass matrix, independent of the element's own rule.

detaileddescription.para: An element evaluates its stiffness and internal forces at the quadrature points of its own rule, which for a reduced-integration element is one order below full. The consistent mass $\mathbf{M}_e = \int \rho\, \mathbf{N}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{N}\, dV$ cannot be integrated that way: it has rank at most (number of quadrature points) $\times$ (number of components), so a reduced 20-node hexahedron, with 8 points, yields a mass of rank 24 out of 60. In the dynamic tangent $\mathbf{K} + \mathbf{M} / (\beta \Delta t^2)$ the stiffness hides that; wherever the mass is solved on its own the initial acceleration $\mathbf{M}\,\mathbf{a}_0 = \mathbf{R}$ of an implicit dynamic analysis the system is singular, and the modes of the null space carry no inertia at all.

The consistent mass is therefore always integrated with the FULL Gauss rule of the element's shape, whatever rule the element uses otherwise. For a full-integration element that is its own rule, and the result is unchanged. The density (and any other inertia coefficient) is a material quantity that lives at the element's own quadrature points; at a point of the mass rule it is taken from the nearest of them in parent coordinates exact for a density that is constant over the element, a piecewise-constant approximation otherwise.

simplesect.para: For the tetrahedra the "full" rules are the element rules themselves (1 point for Tetra4, 4 for Tetra10), which are too low for a mass matrix as well. No tetrahedral element is currently registered; one that is must be given a rule of sufficient order here first.
